slides.0.title: From Carthage to the state system
slides.0.subtitle: Three thousand years of wine, with several breaks
slides.1.title: Carthage and Rome
slides.1.highlights.0.title: The Phoenicians bring wine
slides.1.highlights.0.content: When the Phoenicians founded Carthage they brought winemaking with them. Its ruins lie beside today's capital, Tunis
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Mago the agronomist
slides.1.highlights.1.content: The Carthaginian agronomist Mago wrote on viticulture. His work was translated from Punic into Latin and quoted by Roman writers such as Columella
slides.1.highlights.2.title: After Rome
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Rome took Carthage in 146 BC and production continued. After the Arab conquest it shrank sharply but never disappeared
slides.1.content: Mago's name still appears on Tunisian labels today.
slides.2.title: The French protectorate (1881–1956)
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Starting from almost nothing
slides.2.highlights.0.content: When the protectorate began in 1881, vines and wine were almost absent. Early planting was encouraged by Cardinal Lavigerie
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Phylloxera came late
slides.2.highlights.1.content: While phylloxera ravaged France, Tunisia was spared for a long time. The pest arrived only in 1905 and struck again in 1936
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Producing for France
slides.2.highlights.2.content: About 90% was red, mainly Carignan and Alicante. Output reached 1.8 million hl in 1932, and almost all exports went to France. Overproduction in 1934–36 led to about 15% of vines being uprooted
slides.2.content: This era left southern French grapes and cooperatives, and a structure built for export.
slides.3.title: The first quality rules, and after independence
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Classification under the protectorate
slides.3.highlights.0.content: "Muscat de Tunisie" was created in 1947 and "vin supérieur de Tunisie" in 1948. In 1947 only 25,000 of 600,000 hl were classified
slides.3.highlights.1.title: The first appellations after independence
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Independence came in 1956. A decree of 10 January 1957 regulated wine appellations, and on 18 September 1958 the first two were defined: Muscat de Kélibia and Muscat de Thibar
slides.3.highlights.2.title: From state control to opening up
slides.3.highlights.2.content: After independence the vineyard slowly shrank and the state controlled sales until around 1999. From the late 1990s, investors from France, Germany, Italy and elsewhere came in
slides.3.content: Muscat came first, then the red and rosé regions. You will need this order again in Level 2.

When did phylloxera finally reach Tunisia?

A. Grand Cru Mornag and Mornag
